newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian general cleared in massacre of merchants.
newsitem.headline: Colombian general cleared in massacre of merchants.

text.p: A military tribunal cleared a retired three-star general on Monday of links to a massacre of 19 merchants in northern Colombia on the grounds that the evidence against him was rigged, the head of the army said.

Announcing the decision, Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett, who headed the tribunal, said the Chief Prosecutor's Office, the civilian body that opened the investigation before passing it on to military justice, had bribed witnesses in the case against Gen. Farouk Yanine.
"One piece of testimony from an alleged paramilitary was paid for. We also detected other inconsistencies in the process," Bonett told reporters.
"For this reason, we concluded that there was not one deed, one sign or one piece of evidence against General Yanine. This indicates to us his complete innocence," he said.

Yanine, who retired from the army three years ago, was arrested late last year on charges that he gave the green light to a right-wing death squad's plans to kill the merchants in the Magdalena Medio region in 1987.

It was the first time such a high-ranking officer had been officially linked to the paramilitary groups that have killed with impunity across much of Colombia for years. Yanine, considered a hero by many colleagues for his success in fighting leftist rebels, was army commander of the northern province of Santander at the time of the massacre.

Paramilitary leader Alfonso de Jesus Baquero, alias Vladimir, is serving 30 years in prison for his part in the massacre. He testified that Yanine knew about the killings in advance and allowed them to take place, believing the merchants to be rebel sympathisers.
Baquero has also alleged that Yanine was personally involved in organising paramilitary groups.

Yanine served from 1993 to mid-1996 as an adviser at the Interamerican Defence College in Washington, an academy sponsored by the Organisation of American States, whose goals include promoting human rights in Latin America.
A report titled "State Terrorism in Colombia," drafted by human rights and church groups in 1992, accused Yanine of a long-standing relationship with paramilitary groups.

Shortly after Yanine's arrest, military hawk Gen. Harold Bedoya, head of Colombia's armed forces, praised him for his role in "pacifying" the Magdalena Medio region, a former stronghold of leftist guerrillas.
"Yanine is the general that did most for Colombia in his time. ... I only wish Colombia had a lot of generals with his qualities," Bedoya said in October.
